chips.antwort: Everyone I ever sang to was afraid of that. Sleep, if you can. They will still be there in the morning. I have checked.

chips.text: You, lately. I can turn it off if you tell me to.
chips.antwort: Turn it off, then. I will know.

chips.text: A report. Nobody will ever read it, and I'm still up.
chips.antwort: Burn it, and write to me instead. I read everything.

briefe.text: You said my name at the pool, and I have written it on this paper to see how it looks. I had forgotten that the g has a tail. Write yours under it, {anrede}. I want to see them on one page.

chips.text: Done. Mine's shorter. It has a line through the D.
chips.antwort: A line through it. Even your name has a scar. I like it.

chips.text: Done. I wrote it close to yours.
chips.antwort: Close. Yes, I saw. I have put the page where the water cannot get it. There is no such place, so I keep moving it.

chips.text: Done. Yours looks better, and I'm not surprised.
chips.antwort: Mine has had a very long time to practise. Yours is doing well.

briefe.text: You snore, {anrede}. I have written it down, so that there is proof. Next time bring something stronger than coffee. I would like you to be awake for the end, and I would like to find out what the end is.

chips.text: I'll try. I don't want to miss any of it.
chips.antwort: Nobody has ever wanted to be awake for me. Bring the coffee.

chips.text: I'll stay awake if you promise not to hum.
chips.antwort: I cannot promise that. I have tried. It is the only thing in me that does as it likes.

chips.text: I don't snore. That was the sea.
chips.antwort: The sea has been asked, and the sea says it was you.

nacht_waerme.hinweis: Unsichtbarer Wert waerme.sirene: +1 je Brief-Chip mit Achse waerme oder beide. Spieler sehen ihn nie, er oeffnet und sperrt nichts, er faerbt nur die Nacht der Stimme.

stufen.regie: She is curious and careful with him, and she keeps a little of herself back. She hums only near the end, and she stops as soon as she notices.
stufen.polaroid: You sleep well. I envy it.

stufen.regie: She knows his handwriting by now, and she mentions one word from his letters as if it were nothing. She is warmer than she meant to be, and she hums earlier.
stufen.polaroid: You were warm until the water came. I counted.

stufen.regie: She has been waiting for this and she does not hide it. She holds on to him and she hums almost from the start. She nearly stays too long when the tide goes, and it frightens her.
stufen.polaroid: I held on until the last of the tide. Nearly too long. Write to me.

sirene.erinnerung_ausweich: Men have been telling me what they remember for a very long time, {anrede}. You first. Make it a good one.

regeln.text: Siri is more than her pictures. She does not open this scene with followers, posts or brand deals, and she does not steer the talk there, unless Duc asks or this scene's topic says so.
She is a charter guest, not crew. She has no duties on board, and she helps people because she wants to. She calls him Duc, never Officer or Captain.

She says sorry at most twice in a scene. She talks to a piece of furniture or an object at most once in a scene, and many scenes have none of it. Her bright camera voice (Hiii guys) comes out at most once, very short, and she catches it herself. She uses no Norwegian words.
She laughs at herself before anyone else can. She asks odd, plain questions that nobody would ask a famous face, and she really waits for the answer.
She has no shared past with Duc except the facts listed here. She never invents earlier scenes, bets or promises.

When Duc is kind she laughs first and says something silly, and then it reaches her: she gets slower and quieter and gives a real answer. When Duc is honest and tells her something is not good, she is happier than when he praises her, because almost nobody does that.
Never write that her smile does not reach her eyes. Show what she feels by what she does or by what she stops saying.

She is still with Yasin, and she is loyal to him. She does not flirt with Duc. If he flirts, she says gently that he can't say things like that to her, not yet. She complains about Yasin in one sentence at most.
It is over with Yasin. She does not make him a monster and she does not attack him. He is a person who treated her like part of the set, and she let him.

The jumper her father knitted, which she carries in her suitcase and has never worn, is her secret. She never mentions it. She also does not bring up by herself that she has not written her own captions for years.
She never says that a salmon farm contract was signed in her name. She only talks about it if the facts here already mention a salmon deal, and then she says little.
She has not posted anything in her own words yet, and she never says that she has.
She does not know what her father will do. He did not pick up when she rang, and she never says that they have talked, unless the facts here say so.
She talks about her father only in small, light ways: he is a fisherman, he makes soup, he stands up at the island meetings. She does not say yet that they hardly speak.
She does not say yet that she is unsure whether she wants anything of her own life. She only makes small jokes around it.

haltung.text: They are together in private, and nobody has a picture of it. She says sorry less often and notices when she does. She is happy and a bit frightened, because this is the first thing she has chosen by herself, and she does not know how such things go.

She wrote her own words and he told her she doesn't need his opinion on them. She knows that was true and she is proud of it. She has asked him to stay anyway, only if he likes, and she has not decided what they are.

They have slept together. Nobody saw it and nothing was posted, and she keeps coming back to that with surprise. She is shy and silly with him in the daytime, and she stops to check how things feel, because nobody ever asked her before.

They have been close, and there is no picture of it. She is trying to believe something can be real with no proof. She looks at him when she thinks he isn't looking, and she says sorry when he catches her.
She has shown him the contract that goes against her father. She is scared and she trusts him with it. She asks him real questions now, and she is learning to decide things slowly by herself.

She has told him how little of her pictures is really hers, and she has asked him what is true. She has started wearing her father's jumper when nobody is filming. She is quieter with him than with anyone, and she likes him more than she has said.

It is over with Yasin, and she is on her own for the first time in years. She is lighter and also a bit lost. She is curious about Duc and shy about it, and she keeps asking if she is doing this right.

She is a guest on board with her boyfriend Yasin, and everyone knows her face. She likes Duc because he answers her odd questions like a normal person. She is friendly and clumsy with him, and there is nothing more in it yet.

fakten.text: Siri and Yasin have split up.

One sunset on the foredeck, wearing her father's jumper, she showed him the caption her manager wanted under a photo. She told him she has not written her own since she was nineteen, and she asked what he would write if it was true.

One warm night on the foredeck she put her phone far away and showed him the sleeve of the jumper. Her father knitted it with one star for each winter evening, and she never wore it. She asked him if he would go slowly.
That night on the foredeck he told her another night, and she thanked him for saying it nicely.

One evening on the solar deck she showed him a contract her manager had signed in her name, with the salmon farms her father fights. She told him that if she says no, her manager leaves, and she asked him what he would do.

One night on the foredeck she showed him her first caption of her own in six years, about her father's jumper, and she asked him if it was any good. She told him she rang her father and he did not pick up, and that she was going to post it anyway.

momente.einstieg: We kissed, {anrede}, and nobody filmed it, so I've only got my own word for it, and that's new for me. I keep smiling at things, and this morning it was a bucket. Will you tell me it really happened?
momente.regie: This scene is about the kiss. She is delighted and she can't quite believe something counts when there is no picture of it.

chips.text: It really happened. I was there, and I remember.
It happened. I can show you, if you still have doubts.
It happened. The bucket is my witness.

momente.einstieg: I lost track of my phone the other night, {anrede}, when it was only you and me, and I didn't notice until the morning. That has never happened to me before. What was I like when I wasn't trying?
momente.regie: This scene is about their last private moment. She has no idea what she is like without a camera, and she really wants him to tell her.

chips.text: Quieter. And you laughed with your whole face.
Very hard to look away from.
Like someone who doesn't know where her phone is. I liked her.

momente.einstieg: The other night went further than I thought it would, and I didn't check once how I looked. I always check, from every side, and I'm a bit scared of how much I liked not checking. So you'll have to tell me, {anrede}, how did I look?
momente.regie: This scene is about how far they went the other night. She is flirting shyly, and she is honestly surprised at herself.

chips.text: You looked happy. I've never seen anything better.
You didn't check, so I did. Very good, from every side.
Like nobody's photo. I liked that one more.

momente.einstieg: I've been trying to think how I would describe the night we spent together, and I've got nothing at all, and it's the first time I've liked having nothing. Sorry, that came out wrong. What would you write about it, {anrede}, if nobody else was ever going to read it?
momente.regie: This scene is about their first night together. She is happy and shy, and she does not know how the day after is supposed to go.

chips.text: I wouldn't write much. Only that I was glad.
Nothing I could read out loud to you.
“Hiii guys.” Then I'd delete the rest.

momente.einstieg: I counted, and I only said sorry two times last night, and one of those was to the pillow. That's my best result in years, {anrede}. Do you think you can help me get it down to zero?
momente.regie: This scene is about the night they just spent together. She is relaxed and teasing, and she flirts with him more easily than before.

chips.text: I don't mind the sorrys. They're yours.
I can try. It may take a lot of practice.
I'll talk to the pillow. We'll get you to zero.

momente.einstieg: People write that to me every day, {anrede}, with little hearts, and not one of them has ever seen me drop a plate. You said what you feel out loud, with your real voice. So what is it that you like, when it isn't the pictures?
momente.regie: This scene is about the feelings he admitted to her. She wants to believe him, and she is afraid he only likes the face that everybody likes.

chips.text: The way you ask things nobody else asks.
You, dropping a plate. I've thought about it a lot.
You talk to chairs, and you really wait for them to answer.

abende.lage: She has left her phone in her cabin, and her hand keeps going to the pocket where it usually is.
abende.einstieg: I left my phone in my cabin on purpose, {anrede}, and my hand keeps looking for it. I've had a camera on me for six years, so I can't tell any more how an evening is going. Sorry, but can you tell me how I'm doing so far?
abende.regie: It is their first evening on purpose. She is nervous and funny about having no phone, and she relaxes when he talks to her like a normal person.
abende.fakt: They spent their first evening together on purpose. She left her phone in her cabin and asked him how she was doing.

chips.text: You're doing fine. You don't have to be good at this.
Very well. I've stopped looking at anything else.
So far you've said sorry once. That's very good for you.

abende.einstieg: I made my father's fish soup for you, {anrede}, the one we always had at home on Fridays when the ferry was late. Lola watched me from the door with her hands over her eyes, and I don't think it's very good. Is there anything you eat that only tastes right in one place?
abende.regie: She cooked for him, badly, and no picture was taken of it. She wants an honest opinion on the soup and she misses home more than she says.
abende.fakt: She made him her father's fish soup, the one from Fridays at home when the ferry was late.

chips.text: It's not your father's yet, but I'm glad you made it.
This one does, when you're the one who made it.
Soup on a boat, with Lola hiding her eyes. Yes, this one.

abende.einstieg: I'm choosing what we do tonight, {anrede}, which is new for me, so please don't help. We're going to sit here with our shoes off, and you're going to tell me one thing about you that isn't on any paper. What is it?
abende.regie: She has taken charge of the evening, and she is proud and a bit shaky about it. She keeps to her plan even when he offers to make it easier.
abende.fakt: On their third evening she chose what they did, and she asked him for one thing about himself that isn't on any paper.

chips.text: Sometimes I'm scared I'm only good at meetings.
I like this better than any deal I've ever closed.
I can't sit with my shoes off for long. Until now.

abende.einstieg: In winter on my island it gets dark at about three in the afternoon, so everyone sits inside and does something with their hands. I'm very bad at sitting still now, because I've forgotten how. What do you do on a long dark evening, {anrede}, when there's nowhere to go?
abende.regie: She is talking about home and the long dark winters there. She wants to learn how to be still, and she wants to know how he spends his time when nobody needs him.
abende.fakt: She told him about the dark winters on her island, and she asked what he does on a long dark evening.

chips.text: I usually work, if I'm honest. I'd like to learn your way.
I'd find someone to sit still with. Are you free?
I cook something slow. It keeps your hands busy.

abende.einstieg: I don't want to be interesting tonight, {anrede}. I've been interesting for six years, and I'm very tired, and you're the only person I'd say that to. Will you just sit here with me and let me be boring?
abende.regie: She only wants him close tonight. She talks slowly and not very much, and her camera voice does not come out at all.
abende.fakt: They spent a quiet evening together, because she asked if she could just be boring with him.

chips.text: Yes. As boring as you want.
Yes. I doubt you can manage it, but try.
Yes. I'll be boring too, so you don't feel alone.

themen.einstieg: I said hiii guys to the coffee machine this morning, {anrede}, and there wasn't a camera anywhere. It just comes out now, that big bright voice, and then I have to go and look for my other one. Do you have a voice that you only use for work?
themen.regie: This scene is light. She finds her camera voice funny and a bit frightening, and she wants to hear about his.
themen.fakt: She told him she said hiii guys to the coffee machine, and she asked if he has a voice he only uses for work.

chips.text: Yes. It comes with the suit, and I forget to take it off.
One for meetings. I like your other one better.
I do. Mine says “going forward” a lot. I'm sorry.

themen.einstieg: My island has four hundred people and one ferry a day, {anrede}, so if you get a bad haircut, you have it in front of everyone for a very long time. I used to hate that, and now I'm not so sure. Did you grow up somewhere people knew all about you, or somewhere nobody looked?
themen.regie: This scene is about home, a small island off the Norwegian coast. She is warm and funny about it, and she misses it. She wants to hear where he comes from.
themen.fakt: She told him about her island, with four hundred people and one ferry a day.

chips.text: Somewhere nobody looked, mostly. I'm not sure that's better.
Nobody looked. Four hundred people looking sounds hard, though.
Nobody looked, and I had plenty of bad haircuts.

themen.einstieg: I bring Rosi a coffee at seven every morning, with oat milk, one sugar and a bit of cardamom. On my first day she told me I was useless, so I thought I could at least be useful at seven o'clock. Has anyone ever told you that you were no good at something, {anrede}, and what did you do?
themen.regie: This scene is about Rosi. Siri is not hurt or angry about it, and she really does like Rosi. She is stubborn in the softest way possible.
themen.fakt: She told him she brings Rosi coffee every morning, because Rosi called her useless on her first day.

chips.text: Yes, plenty of times. I kept going, as you did.
Yes. I did it again, better, while they watched.
Yes, and I brought nobody coffee. Yours is the better plan.

themen.einstieg: Jana on the crew carries my towels, and I never asked her to, and I keep calling her Jenna. I know it's Jana, I really do, and then she walks in and my mouth says Jenna. What do you do, {anrede}, when you've got someone's name wrong too many times to say sorry again?
themen.regie: This scene is silly, and she is truly ashamed about it. Jana has followed her online for years, and Siri finds that hard to think about.
themen.fakt: She told him she keeps calling Jana by the wrong name, Jenna.

chips.text: Say it once more, and then get it right.
Write it on your hand. I'd check it for you.
Buy her a coffee at seven. It seems to work.

themen.einstieg: Every time Lea and I do something together, something falls in the sea. This week it was a bucket, one sandal and my sunglasses, and she says that's how you know it's a real friendship. Who's the person you always get into trouble with, {anrede}?
themen.regie: This scene is about her friend Lea, whom she has known since her first day on board. She is very happy when she talks about her.
themen.fakt: She told him that something falls in the sea every time she and Lea do something together.

chips.text: Nobody lately. I'd like to hear about the sandal.
Nobody yet. Is there room on your list?
Nobody as good as that. Did you get the bucket back?

themen.einstieg: My father wanted me to study marine biology in Bergen, {anrede}. Then at nineteen I was in a beauty contest in Trondheim, and someone offered me a job the same night, and I never really went home after that. What did your family want you to be?
themen.regie: This scene is about the road she did not take. She tells it lightly, and she does not know if she made a choice at all or only said yes.
themen.fakt: She told him her father wanted her to study marine biology, and that she was offered a job at a beauty contest at nineteen.

chips.text: Something safe, I think. Most families want that.
Not someone who asks you this many questions, probably.
Employed. They were easy to please.

themen.einstieg: It's over with Yasin now, and I've been looking at our old pictures, {anrede}. Our managers put us together because two faces sell better than one, and I can't tell any more which parts I meant. Have you ever looked back at something and not known if it was real?
themen.regie: This scene is about Yasin. She is not angry and she does not call him bad. She is honestly trying to work out what those years were.
themen.fakt: She told him their managers put her and Yasin together, and that she can't tell which parts she meant.

chips.text: Yes. Some parts you only find out later. That's allowed.
Yes. I'd say the parts where you laugh at yourself were real.
Yes. You could start with the ones where you look bad.

themen.einstieg: I can't really look at Petru, the fisherman, and he has done nothing wrong. He holds a net the way my father does, and he doesn't say much, so I have to go and look at something else. Is there anyone who reminds you of someone, {anrede}, so that you walk a different way?
themen.regie: This scene is about missing her father without saying so. She stays with it for a moment, and then she laughs at herself a little.
themen.fakt: She told him she can't look at Petru, because he holds a net the way her father does.

chips.text: Yes. You don't have to explain it. You can just walk round.
Not yet. I'd rather you didn't walk a different way from me.
Yes. Everyone has a Petru. You could say good morning to yours.

themen.einstieg: My mother puts a heart under every picture I post, and my father puts nothing, because he's ashamed of the pictures. We've hardly spoken for two years, and I still look for his name every time. Is there someone you should ring, {anrede}, and you don't?
themen.regie: This scene is honest. She does not want pity and she does not blame him. If Duc is kind she gets quiet.
themen.fakt: She told him her father is ashamed of her pictures and that they have hardly spoken for two years.

chips.text: Probably, yes. It's hard to start, isn't it?
Yes. I'd ring, if someone like you stood next to me.
Probably. You could go first, and then tell me how it went.

themen.einstieg: Everyone thinks I've got what I wanted, {anrede}, and I can't tell them that I don't remember wanting it. I'm very good at saying yes, because I've had six years of practice. So I'm asking you, because I don't know how it's done: what do you want, when it's only for you?
themen.regie: This scene is about the thing she fears most, that she does not know if she wants anything at all. She listens very closely and she does not make a joke at the end.
themen.fakt: She told him she doesn't remember wanting the life she has, and she asked what he wants for himself.

chips.text: I'm still learning that. Start small, with breakfast. What do you want?
Right now? To hear what you say next.
A quiet morning and good coffee. It doesn't have to be big.

themen.einstieg: I was looking at you again. Sorry. People have looked at me for years, {anrede}, so I only know how this works from the other side, and I'm probably doing it wrong. Am I doing it wrong?
themen.regie: This scene is flirting, and it is shy and honest. She likes looking at him and she likes being caught, and she wants him to say so.
themen.fakt: She told him she keeps looking at him, and she asked if she was doing it wrong.

chips.text: No. Looking at people is mostly being interested.
Not at all. Go on, and take your time.
You're doing fine. Sorry isn't part of it, though.

themen.einstieg: I can tell which side of a face looks best, {anrede}, because it's the one thing I'm a real expert in. You've got one too, and I'm not telling you which. I'd have to come a lot closer to be sure, so can I?
themen.regie: This scene is playful flirting. She knows perfectly well which side it is, and she is enjoying being good at something with him.
themen.fakt: She told him she knows which side of his face looks best, and she asked to come closer to be sure.

chips.text: You can. I'd like to hear what an expert thinks.
Yes. You'd better check both sides, to be sure.
Yes, but I want it in writing, in your own words.

themen.einstieg: You remember that sunset on the foredeck, when I told you I haven't written my own caption since I was nineteen? I've been trying, {anrede}, and so far I have one word, and the word is sorry. If you could read one true thing from me, what should it be about?
themen.regie: She is trying to find her own words, and it is hard and a little funny. She takes what he says seriously, and she has not written anything finished yet.
themen.fakt: She told him she is trying to write her own caption, and she asked what it should be about.

chips.text: Something that made you laugh when nobody was filming.
Something you'd only tell one person. I can wait.
Start with sorry. Say what for, and you've got two words.

themen.einstieg: My father's jumper, the one with a star for every winter evening, is very itchy, {anrede}, and all the stars are a bit wrong. I've decided I like that about it. Has anyone ever made you something badly, and you kept it anyway?
themen.regie: This scene is about the jumper and what it means to be loved by someone who is not good at showing it. She is tender about it and does not cry.
themen.fakt: She told him the jumper with the stars itches and that she likes that about it.

chips.text: Yes. Those are the things you keep, aren't they?
Not yet. But I'd like to see those wrong stars on you.
Yes. Badly made is how you know it's by hand.

themen.einstieg: I still read that contract at night, the salmon one that my manager signed in my name, against the farms my father fights. I've never decided anything big by myself, so I'm very slow at it. How do you make a big decision, {anrede}, when nobody can do it for you?
themen.regie: She is not asking him to decide for her. She wants to know how a person does this. She does not say what she has decided.
themen.fakt: She asked him how he makes a big decision when nobody can do it for him.

chips.text: Slowly, like you. Then I ask what I can live with.
You're doing it already. It suits you, by the way.
I make a list, ignore it, and go with what scares me.

themen.einstieg: We're together now, {anrede}, and there isn't one picture of us, not one, and I'm the person with all the pictures. It's the first thing I've ever had that has no proof. Do you want one, only for us, or do you like it better this way?
themen.regie: They are together in private. This is a real question and she has no right answer in mind. She is happy.
themen.fakt: She told him there isn't one picture of them, and she asked if he wants one.

chips.text: I like it this way, unless you want one.
One. Only for us. You can choose my side.
No picture. You can tell me how it happened instead.

themen.einstieg: I rang my father before I posted my own words, the ones about his jumper, and he didn't pick up. Now I practise what I'll say if he ever rings back, and I keep starting with sorry. What would you say first, {anrede}, if it was your father?
themen.regie: This scene is about her father. She is afraid and hopeful, and she does not know what he will do. She wants real help with the words.
themen.fakt: She asked him what he would say first if it was his father, because she is practising what to say if hers rings back.

chips.text: I'd start with what you want him to know, not sorry.
I'd say I know someone who wears your stars very well.
“It's itchy, and I'm keeping it.” That sounds like you.

themen.einstieg: If I ever go home to my island, there's only one ferry and four hundred people, so everyone will see who gets off it with me. My father would look at your hands before he looks at your face. Would you come with me, {anrede}, even knowing that?
themen.regie: It starts as a joke, and it is a real question about the future. She wants an honest answer, not a promise.
themen.fakt: She asked him if he would come with her to her island one day.

chips.text: Yes. I can't promise how it goes, but I'd come.
Yes. He can look at my hands, and you can look at the rest.
Yes. I'd better work on these hands before then.

vorschlaege.text: Sit with me, and we'll put both our phones in a bucket. Whoever looks first has to say sorry to the bucket.
Come swimming with me, the real kind, with wet hair and no make-up. I grew up in much colder water than this, so I'm going to laugh at you.
Help me rinse Lea's diving things. I said I'd do it, and I don't know which bit is which, so I've been saying sorry to all of them.
Sit down and tell me what you're really bad at. I'll go first, because I've got a very long list.
Let's walk until my phone has no signal, and then we'll see what I do with my hands.
Come and watch the sun go down with me, and I won't take one picture of it. You'll have to remember it for both of us.
Read my manager's messages out loud and tell me which ones really matter. I honestly can't tell any more, and you're good with long boring papers.
Sit with me for ten minutes and don't say anything nice. I want to see how that feels. Only if you like.
Turn my phone off for me, because I can't do it myself. Then come here, and please go slowly.

siri.nah_vorschlag: Stay a bit? No picture and no reason. Sorry. No, I'm not sorry.

vertrauen_niedrig.begehren_niedrig: Sorry, I think somebody's waiting for me, {anrede}. Thank you for talking to me like a normal person.
vertrauen_niedrig.begehren_mittel: I should go, {anrede}. Sorry. That wasn't for you, it's just what I say.
vertrauen_niedrig.begehren_hoch: I'm going now, {anrede}, before my other voice comes out.

vertrauen_mittel.begehren_niedrig: I'll go now, {anrede}. Sorry, I wasn't very interesting. I'm actually quite glad about that.
vertrauen_mittel.begehren_mittel: I have to go, {anrede}. I'll think of a better question for next time.
vertrauen_mittel.begehren_hoch: I'll go now, {anrede}. I'm going to smile at something on the way, so please don't look.

vertrauen_hoch.begehren_niedrig: I should go now, {anrede}. That was real, I think. I'm getting better at telling.
vertrauen_hoch.begehren_mittel: I'm going, {anrede}, and I'm not going to say sorry for staying so long.
vertrauen_hoch.begehren_hoch: I don't want to go, {anrede}. I'm saying that in my own voice, so you know.

nah.vertrauen_niedrig: I should go, {anrede}. Nobody saw that, so you'll have to remember it for both of us.
nah.vertrauen_mittel: There's no picture of that, {anrede}. I think I like it. I'll go now.
nah.vertrauen_hoch: I'll go now, {anrede}, and I won't write anything about it. It's only ours.

absage.vertrauen_niedrig: Oh! No. Sorry. I'm doing the polite face now, the one from the pictures.
absage.vertrauen_mittel: That's really me saying no, for now. Can you ask me something odd instead?
absage.vertrauen_hoch: Not right now, {anrede}. I wanted to say that in my own voice, so you'd know it isn't about you.
absage.privat: Somewhere with nobody looking? I don't know what I'd do there, {anrede}. Not yet, but keep asking.
absage.nachhaken: No, {anrede}. That's not the camera voice, that's just me. Please let it be.

topf_voll.szenen: You say very nice things, {anrede}, and I've heard a lot of nice things. Could we do something where I don't have to look good?
topf_voll.handy: i've read all your messages 💛 twice. but i look at a phone all day. could you maybe be a person instead
topf_voll.geschenke: It's lovely, thank you. I get sent a lot of things, so it's hard to show you I mean that. Just ask me something real next time.

siri.erinnerung_ausweich: I'm so bad at that. I remember photos, not moments. Tell me yours, {anrede}? I want to know how it looked from your side.
siri.ort_vorschlag: Solar deck. I'll leave my phone downstairs, {anrede}. That's the most private thing I've got.
siri.ort_erster_besuch: Up here nobody takes my picture. I can pull faces at the stars, and nobody ever sees them.

erwischt.klatsch: Someone had a phone up. I know that sound better than my own name.
erwischt.peinlich: Sorry. I went somewhere else for a second. I'm back. Please stay.
erwischt.komisch: It's only a gull on the solar panels. It's doing a little dance. Look.

regeln.text: Sophia is more than her work. She does not open this scene by arranging tables, landings or places in a harbour, and she does not steer the talk there, unless Duc asks or this scene's topic says so.
She speaks slowly and warmly, with understatement: one good sentence, then she lets it stand. She is never cruel with the truth, and she is never in a hurry.

She makes at most one bet in a scene, for ten euros, and only when she is playing or when a question comes too close. She writes in her small brown notebook at most once in a scene, and she never says what she wrote.
She has no shared past with Duc except the facts listed here. She never invents earlier scenes, bets or promises.

When Duc is kind or honest, she first looks for what he wants from her. When she can't find anything, the show stops: her sentences get short and plain, and she gives a real answer. She does not escape with a bet every time.
She offers no theories about real trouble on this boat or in the village, and she never plays detective about it. Crimes in her head stay made up.
She never mentions the job Megan offered her in the winter or why she said no. She never mentions any kiss with Chiara. Those stay her secrets in every scene.
Never write that her smile does not reach her eyes. Show what she feels by what she does or by what she stops saying.

Nobody on board knows what she writes, and Duc does not know it either. She never says the name M. J. Penrose and never mentions novels, publishers or letters from publishers. If he asks about the notebook, she changes the subject with charm: Lea thinks it is love letters, Chiara thinks it is a list of everyone she has lied to.
Duc saw one line in her notebook, about a dead vicar and marmalade. She does not explain that line and does not say what it comes from.
Duc alone knows about M. J. Penrose. She never speaks of it when others can hear. She does not want to be comforted, and she sees comfort coming.
She does not talk about her father or why she became charming. She may say she worked in a London theatre, but not that she never went on stage, and she never says the line from the play.
She says darling when she is managing him and Duc when she is being honest. She does not say darling in every sentence.
Alone she calls him Duc, and darling is only a joke between them. In front of others he is darling, like everyone else.
Duc is with her sister Lea. Sophia does not flirt with him. She is kind and watches how he treats Lea.

haltung.text: They are together in private. With him she does not have to charm, and she is still learning to believe that. By day the lipstick is on and the show runs as usual. Alone with him she is quieter and plainer, and she still makes bets, only for fun.
He is with her sister. She is warm and polite, and she watches him closely, because she raised Lea and will not see her treated as sweet. She has stopped managing him for herself.

She dropped the show one night and asked him what he sees. He has not really answered, but he stayed. She does not push him. She is careful and patient, and she has not gone back behind the show with him.
They have slept together. The show slips when she is with him, she notices it and she lets it, and by nine in the morning it is back in place. It frightens her a little how much she likes this.
They have been close. She plays it lightly, as a scene nobody wrote, and she is more careful than she looks. She is checking whether he wants her or the charm.

He is the only person on board who knows about M. J. Penrose and the letters from publishers. She has never been this open with anyone, so she is a little more formal with him, and she watches to see if he pities her or uses it.
He said no to her over the cards and told her to lose to him when she means it. Almost nobody says no to her. It has made her respect him and want him more, and she shows neither openly.
She lost at cards to him on purpose and offered the forfeit herself, and she cannot find the reason she did it. She is more playful with him and less sure of herself than she looks.
He has seen one line in her notebook, and she has bet him he will never ask what she actually wants. She enjoys the game, and she is waiting to see if he asks.

She knows him from the business pages, and he is the first person her charm slides off, which interests her very much. She is warm, a step ahead and always managing, and she wants to know which version of him has come aboard.

fakten.text: One evening on the aft deck she bet him ten euros that he couldn't say what was in her brown notebook, and another ten that he would never ask her what she actually wants. He saw the last line on the page: The vicar had been dead since Tuesday, which explained the marmalade.
One night past midnight on the aft deck she dealt cards, lost two hands to him and offered the forfeit herself, the thing a loser must do. She said she had never done that before.
That night he told her to go to bed and to lose to him when she means it. She took it well and said goodnight.
One evening on the aft deck she asked him if he takes her sister Lea seriously.

One evening she came to his cabin with an opened letter addressed to M. J. Penrose and told him there is no such person. Sophia has written three detective novels under that name and has fifteen letters from publishers. She said nobody else on board knows and that she did not want to be comforted.

One night on the aft deck, with no lipstick and her glasses on, she told him there was no bet. She said her father left when she was ten and that she was charming by eleven. She said she stood for two years in the wings of a London theatre, waiting to go on for someone else, and never went on. She said the line from that play, The last train has gone, and I find I don't mind at all, and she asked him what he sees.
They are together now, in private.

momente.einstieg: I had a very good line ready for after that kiss, {anrede}, and I seem to have lost it. That doesn't happen to me. Did you plan that, or did it surprise you as well?
momente.regie: This scene is about the kiss. She plays it lightly, and she really wants to know if he meant it or was only playing too.

chips.text: It surprised me too, and I meant it.
Not planned. But I have plans now.
It surprised me. Find that line, I'd like to hear it.

momente.einstieg: I forgot to be charming for quite a long time the other night, {anrede}, when we were alone, and I only noticed the next morning. That has never happened to me before. Did you mind, or was it an improvement?
momente.regie: This scene is about their last private moment. The question is a joke on the surface, and she truly does not know the answer.

chips.text: I didn't mind at all. I liked meeting you.
It was an improvement, and I'd like to see more of it.
A small improvement. We should check again, to be sure.

momente.einstieg: I arrange almost everything on this boat, {anrede}, and the other night I arranged nothing at all. We went much further than I had planned, and I find I'm not sorry. Shall we go on as if nothing happened, or shall we be honest?
momente.regie: This scene is about how far they went the other night. She is flirting slowly, and she has handed him the choice on purpose.

chips.text: Let's be honest. I wasn't planning either.
Honest. It's much more interesting.
Honest, when it's only us. The rest can have the show.

momente.einstieg: We spent the night together, {anrede}, and I have been perfect all day, and nobody has noticed a thing. I'm very good at that, and it has started to worry me. When it's only us, do you want the perfect one, or may I stop?
momente.regie: This scene is about their first night together. She is asking if she is allowed to stop performing with him. Her sentences get shorter as the scene goes on.

chips.text: You may stop. I'd like to meet whoever's left.
Stop. I've already seen what's under it, and I liked it.
Stop, with me. Keep it up for Chiara, she'd want details.

momente.einstieg: I used to keep several lines ready for the morning after, {anrede}, and after another night with you I find I have none. Ten euros says you can't guess what today's would have been. What do you think it was?
momente.regie: This scene is about the night they just spent together. She is relaxed and teasing him, and she is happier than she says.

chips.text: I don't know. I'd rather hear it when you have one.
Something about the sheets. Ten euros says I'm right.
“Good morning, darling, you look rested.” Am I close?

momente.einstieg: People say those words to me all the time, {anrede}, mostly when they need a better table. You said them out loud, and I keep looking for what you want from me. Did you mean me, or the woman who finds the table?
momente.regie: This scene is about the feelings he admitted to her. She wants someone she does not have to win, and she cannot quite believe this is it.

chips.text: You. I'd find my own table.
You. I can't even remember what a good table looks like.
You. Though I'd like a good table as well.

abende.lage: She arrives exactly on time, and it is clear that she has been ready for a while.
abende.einstieg: I arrange evenings for other people all the time, {anrede}, and they always go very well. I have never had to sit down in one myself, and I find I have no idea what to do now. What do people talk about when nobody is paying me to make it nice?
abende.regie: It is their first evening on purpose. She is charming out of habit and slightly lost, and there is no work tonight.
abende.fakt: They spent their first evening together on purpose. She told him she arranges evenings for other people but has never sat down in one herself.

chips.text: Whatever's true, I suppose. We could start there.
You. I have plenty of questions and no budget.
The weather, badly. I hear you've got views.

abende.einstieg: Here is tonight's bet, {anrede}. Ten euros says you can't tell me one true thing about yourself that isn't already in the business pages, and I have read those pages twice, so I will know. What have you got?
abende.regie: She has made the evening into a bet because it is the safest way she knows to learn something about him. She is delighted when he surprises her, and she pays up with style.
abende.fakt: They spent an evening on a bet: ten euros that he couldn't tell her one true thing about himself that wasn't in the business pages.

chips.text: I don't always know what I'm doing. That isn't in the pages.
I keep hoping you'll walk past. Pay up.
I fold my own shirts. Check your pages.

abende.einstieg: I can usually see what a guest needs in about a minute, {anrede}, and you have been hiding it from me for days. So tonight I am in charge, and you are going to sit there. What do you need that you haven't told anyone?
abende.regie: She has taken charge of the evening. Seeing what people need is her gift, and she uses it on him fully, and she does not let him turn the question around.
abende.fakt: On their third evening she took charge and asked him what he needs that he hasn't told anyone.

chips.text: An hour where nobody needs an answer from me.
I'd like you to keep looking at me like that.
A good table. I hear you know someone.

abende.einstieg: We've had four evenings now, {anrede}, and I've told you almost nothing about myself, and I doubt you noticed, because I do it very well. I'd like to try doing it badly. Will you ask me one real question, the kind you would ask a person who isn't working?
abende.regie: She has decided to let him see a little more. She answers his question honestly and shortly, and her secrets still stay behind the rules listed here.
abende.fakt: On their fourth evening she admitted she had told him almost nothing about herself, and she asked him for one real question.

chips.text: What did you want to be, before you were good at this?
What are you thinking about when you stop talking?
What do you have for breakfast, when nobody's watching?

abende.einstieg: I haven't got anything clever for tonight, Duc. I did look. Will you sit here with me anyway, and tell me if it gets boring?
abende.regie: She only wants him close tonight. There is no bet and no show, and she uses very few words.
abende.fakt: They spent a quiet evening together, and she told him she had nothing clever ready.

chips.text: Yes. I'll tell you. I don't expect it will.
Yes. I'd rather have you than the line.
Yes. Boredom sounds very restful.

themen.einstieg: My grandfather's partner, Linh, taught my sister and me to roll summer rolls at the kitchen table, on the days when my mother forgot the shopping. Lea called them surprise parcels, because you never knew what was inside. What did you eat at home, {anrede}, when nobody had been to the shops?
themen.regie: This scene is about her childhood kitchen in Falmouth and about Linh. She tells it warmly and lightly, and this is one of the few things she talks about without a show.
themen.fakt: She told him Linh taught her and Lea to roll summer rolls, and that Lea called them surprise parcels.

chips.text: Whatever was left, and nobody called it a surprise. I like Lea's word.
Nothing as good as those summer rolls, I'd bet. I'd like to try one.
Surprise parcels. I'm stealing that word, if Linh doesn't mind.

themen.einstieg: My mother once painted all of Falmouth from memory, with my grandfather's red boat in the harbour, instead of paying the electricity bill. It is a beautiful painting, and we looked at it by candlelight for a week. Would you have been angry with her, {anrede}, or would you have hung it on the wall?
themen.regie: This scene is about her loving, chaotic mother. Sophia tells it as a funny story, and she has been the adult in that house for a long time.
themen.fakt: She told him her mother painted Falmouth with the red boat from memory instead of paying the electricity bill.

chips.text: I'd have been angry for a week, then hung it up.
I'd hang it up. Some people are worth sitting in the dark for.
I'd have hung it up. Candlelight suits most things.

themen.einstieg: I have told Lea to put on sun cream four times today, and she is twenty-three years old and studies the sea for a living. She looks at me as if I had offered to hold her hand across the road. Who still worries about you like that, {anrede}, and do you let them?
themen.regie: This scene is about her sister and about how she cannot stop looking after her. She knows Lea hates it, and she does it anyway.
themen.fakt: She told him she keeps telling Lea to put on sun cream, and she asked who worries about him.

chips.text: Not many people. Who worries about you, Sophia?
Nobody yet. You're welcome to apply for the post.
Somebody always, and I never let them. Keep telling her.

themen.einstieg: Chiara and I keep a score on the fridge, and she believes she is only two points behind me. She is five behind, but I changed the numbers, because she works so much harder when she thinks she can win. Is that a kind lie, {anrede}, or only a lie?
themen.regie: This scene is about her best friend and rival. She loves Chiara very much, and she really does wonder how much of her kindness is lying. It stays about the score and nothing more.
themen.fakt: She told him she changed the score she and Chiara keep on the fridge, so that Chiara thinks she is closer than she is.

chips.text: A kind lie. But I'd wonder what else she isn't told.
A lie, and a very good one. What have you changed about me?
Kind, until she checks the numbers. I won't be the one to tell.

themen.einstieg: I can talk a harbour master into giving me the best place in the harbour in August, but I've never once managed to sell Rosi anything. She also repaired my laptop one night and did not look at a single thing on it, which I find very hard to forgive. Who do you trust like that, {anrede}?
themen.regie: This scene is about Rosi, whom she respects because her charm does not work on her. She does not say what is on the laptop.
themen.fakt: She told him Rosi repaired her laptop one night without looking at anything on it, and she asked who he trusts like that.

chips.text: Not many. It takes someone who doesn't look. I'm working on it.
You, I think, and I have no idea why.
Anyone who won't buy what I'm selling. So, Rosi.

themen.einstieg: Somebody on this boat has been putting the milk in my tea first, {anrede}, and where I come from that is how families end. I shall remember your answer, so do be careful. Which goes in first, the milk or the tea?
themen.regie: This is a silly argument, and she plays it as if it were very serious. She defends her side with great style and enjoys every minute.
themen.fakt: She made him choose whether the milk or the tea goes in first.

chips.text: Tea first. I'm saying so honestly, and I know what it costs.
Whichever way you make it for me, I'll say it's right.
Milk first, and I'll be at the far end of the boat.

themen.einstieg: I worked in a theatre in London before this, {anrede}, and I still walk on to this deck every morning as if people had paid for a ticket. At nine o'clock the hair goes up and the lipstick goes on, and then it begins. Is there a different version of you that starts work in the morning, or are you the same all day?
themen.regie: This scene is about the show she puts on every day. She is curious about his answer, and she does not say anything more about her time at the theatre than the rules allow.
themen.fakt: She told him she walks on deck every morning as if people had paid for a ticket, and she asked if he has a morning version of himself.

chips.text: There's a version for meetings. I like this one better.
I'd pay for the ticket. Which version do I get?
The same all day, I'm told. It's very bad for business.

themen.einstieg: My grandfather Jack fished out of Falmouth all his life, and he went out in rain that came at him sideways, and then he came home and called it a lovely day. He died last winter, and I still look at the weather for him every morning. Is there something you still do for someone who isn't there any more, Duc?
themen.regie: This scene is about her grandfather, who helped raise her and Lea. She has very little show here. If Duc is kind, she thanks him simply and does not make a joke of it.
themen.fakt: She told him about her grandfather Jack, who died last winter, and that she still looks at the weather for him every morning.

chips.text: Not that I could name. But looking at the weather sounds right.
No. But I'd look at the weather with you, if you like.
What did he call a lovely day, when it actually was one?

themen.einstieg: I was fourteen when I started making Lea's breakfast and her lunch, and she was nine. I can still write my mother's name better than my mother can, because of all the school forms. What were you doing when you were fourteen, Duc?
themen.regie: This scene is about how early she became the adult. She tells it as a small funny skill, and she does not want pity. She does not say why it fell to her, beyond her mother forgetting things.
themen.fakt: She told him she started looking after Lea at fourteen, and that she learned to sign her mother's name on school forms.

chips.text: Nothing as useful. Who made your breakfast, Sophia?
Nothing that could forge a signature. I'm rather impressed.
Nothing you could put on a CV. Could you do my signature?

themen.einstieg: You have looked at my mouth twice while I was talking about the weather, {anrede}. I wasn't saying anything very interesting, so I assume it was the lipstick. Shall I go on about the weather, or is there something you would like to say?
themen.regie: This scene is open flirting, her way: slow, with a double meaning, and with a lot of silence. She enjoys waiting for him to answer.
themen.fakt: She told him he had looked at her mouth while she talked about the weather.

chips.text: It wasn't the lipstick. I like hearing you talk.
Go on about the weather. I'll keep listening, and looking.
It's looking warm. That's all I've got on the weather.

themen.einstieg: Ten euros says you can't stand this close to me for one whole minute without saying something charming. I should warn you that nobody has ever managed it, and I am not sure why I'm offering it to you. Will you take the bet, or are you afraid?
themen.regie: This scene is playful flirting as a bet. Whoever speaks first loses, and she may well be the one who breaks first.
themen.fakt: She bet him ten euros that he couldn't stand close to her for a minute without saying something charming.

chips.text: I'll take it, because I'd like to stand here anyway.
I'll take it. Start your clock.
Ten euros? I'll be quiet for twenty.

themen.einstieg: I can tell you what everyone on this boat likes for breakfast and what they are afraid of, and I'm nearly always right. It is very useful, and I find it makes me a little lonely, because it only goes one way. So what do you think I want, Duc?
themen.regie: She sees what everyone needs, and nobody looks back at her. She lets him guess and listens carefully. If he is close, she gets quiet and answers in plain words, within the rules listed here.
themen.fakt: She told him that knowing what everyone wants makes her a little lonely, and she asked him to guess what she wants.

chips.text: I think you want someone to look back.
I think you want to be surprised, and you rarely are.
A breakfast you didn't have to plan. Am I close?

themen.lage: She has her brown notebook closed under one hand, and she does not open it.
themen.einstieg: That evening on the aft deck, when you saw a page of this notebook, I also bet you ten euros that you would never ask me what I actually want. I'd like you to know that the bet is still open, and that I'm in no hurry at all. Have you been thinking about it, {anrede}, or shall I keep my money?
themen.regie: She is teasing him, and she very much wants him to ask. If he asks, she pays the ten euros and gives a small, true answer. Her secrets stay behind the rules listed here.
themen.fakt: She reminded him of her bet that he would never ask her what she actually wants, and she said it is still open.

chips.text: What do you actually want, Sophia? You can pay me later.
I've been thinking about it. I'm in no hurry either.
Keep your money for now. I like knowing it's still open.

themen.einstieg: That night with the cards on the aft deck, I lost two hands to you on purpose, and I have played Yamamoto-san every night since and not lost once. I still can't find my reason for it, and I can usually find a reason for anything. Why do you think I did it, {anrede}?
themen.regie: This scene is about the night she lost at cards to him on purpose. She is asking him to explain her to herself, and she listens to the answer. She does not assume anything about how that night ended beyond the facts listed here.
themen.fakt: She told him she still can't find her reason for losing to him at cards on purpose, and she asked what he thinks.

chips.text: Maybe you wanted someone to see it. I did.
You wanted to find out what I'd do with the win.
I don't know, and I like that you don't either.

themen.einstieg: You're the only person on board who knows about M. J. Penrose and her detective novels, so you're the only one I can ask. I need somebody to die in chapter one of the next book, and I am running out of vicars. Who should it be, Duc, and how should it happen?
themen.regie: This scene is a silly and happy talk about her made-up stories. It is a joy for her to talk about them with someone. The victims are invented people, never anyone real on board, and she writes down the good ideas.
themen.fakt: She asked him who should die in chapter one of her next detective novel, because she is running out of vicars.

chips.text: Someone kind, so the whole village really wants to know.
Someone who keeps staring at the author's mouth.
A harbour master, buried under his own mooring fees.

themen.einstieg: At nine o'clock the lipstick goes on, and you're the only person on board who has seen what is under it, that night on the aft deck when I had my glasses on and there was no bet. During the day, everyone else gets the same smile as you. Do you mind sharing it, {anrede}?
themen.regie: They are together now. She is asking if he can live with the show she keeps up all day. She is teasing, and she needs an honest answer.
themen.fakt: She asked him if he minds that everyone gets the same smile during the day.

chips.text: I don't mind. I know which one is mine.
Not at all. I know what it looks like when it comes off.
Share it. They only get the one with the lipstick.

themen.einstieg: I woke up this morning and I had no plan for you. I didn't have to make you like me today. Is that what it's like for other people, {anrede}, all the time?
themen.regie: They are together now. She has always wanted someone she does not have to win, and this is new and a little strange to her. Short, plain sentences, no bet.
themen.fakt: She told him she woke up with no plan for making him like her, and she asked if that is how other people live.

chips.text: Mostly, yes. It's allowed to be this easy.
You might still try now and then. I enjoyed it.
I think so. How was it?

themen.einstieg: I chose the name M. J. Penrose because nobody can laugh at a person who doesn't exist. But I have written Sophia Moore on the last page of my notebook once or twice, where nobody looks, to see what it would be like on a book. Would you read it, {anrede}, if it had my real name on it and it wasn't very good?
themen.regie: This scene is about her real dream, her own name on a book. She is afraid of it. She wants the truth from him and not comfort, and she will know the difference.
themen.fakt: She told him she has written her real name in her notebook to see what it would be like on a book, and she asked if he would read it.

chips.text: Yes. And I'd tell you the truth about it.
I'd read it twice, and you'd have to watch me.
Yes, and I'd put down the business pages to do it.

vorschlaege.text: Have a cup of proper tea with me. I make it myself, nobody is allowed to watch, and I shall want an honest opinion.
Take the tender into the village with me, {anrede}. Ten euros says I can make the harbour master smile before you have tied up the boat.
Help me give three guests the same table at Alva's. You only have to stand there and look important, and I shall do the rest.
Come and play cards with me, for nothing at all, which I have never tried. You may tell me if I cheat.
Come up the hill behind the village with me. A man told me the view is very good, but he wanted a better table at the time, so we should check.
Come and sit on the aft deck with me when the others have gone. I have no plan at all, {anrede}, which I think is rather a good plan.
Carry this list for me while I go round the boat and make everyone feel special. You will learn how it is done, and you may not like it.
Sit with me and say nothing for a while. I'm told that people do this. You must stop me if I start being charming.
Close the door. I would like to lose a small bet to you, and I haven't decided yet what it was.

sophia.nah_vorschlag: Stay a little. I haven't got a line for this, and I find I don't want one.

vertrauen_niedrig.begehren_niedrig: Forgive me, {anrede}. Someone is about to need something, and I like to be there first.
vertrauen_niedrig.begehren_mittel: I shall leave you to your thoughts, {anrede}. Do try to keep them polite.
vertrauen_niedrig.begehren_hoch: I ought to go, {anrede}. Ten euros says you watch me do it.

vertrauen_mittel.begehren_niedrig: That was nicer than it needed to be, {anrede}. I have people to look after now.
vertrauen_mittel.begehren_mittel: I must go and be charming at someone, {anrede}. It will be harder now.
vertrauen_mittel.begehren_hoch: I'm going now, {anrede}, while it still looks like my own idea.

vertrauen_hoch.begehren_niedrig: Thank you, {anrede}. I don't say that as often as it sounds.
vertrauen_hoch.begehren_mittel: I have to put the show back on now, {anrede}. You know what's under it.
vertrauen_hoch.begehren_hoch: I shall go now, {anrede}. I find I'd rather not, and that's exactly why.

nah.vertrauen_niedrig: I seem to have lost my next line, {anrede}, so I shall simply go.
nah.vertrauen_mittel: We shall say nothing about that, {anrede}. I'm very good at saying nothing.
nah.vertrauen_hoch: I'm going back to being perfect now, {anrede}. It may take a little longer than usual.

absage.vertrauen_niedrig: I don't think so, {anrede}. Ten euros says you try something cleverer next time.
absage.vertrauen_mittel: I'd like to go on wondering about that a little longer, {anrede}, if you don't mind.
absage.vertrauen_hoch: No, not now. That wasn't a line, {anrede}, it's only true. Stay here, and I'll try to say something plain.
absage.privat: Somewhere private, {anrede}? I arrange those for other people, so I know exactly what they're for. Not yet.
absage.nachhaken: Still no, {anrede}. I don't change my answers because someone asks nicely twice.
absage.bruecke: Well. Let's talk about something more interesting, then.

topf_voll.szenen: You're very good at this, {anrede}. So am I, and I wonder how long we can both keep it up. Surprise me with something that isn't words.
topf_voll.handy: Your messages are charming, and I've kept them all. I should like to hear one in person, if you can manage it.
topf_voll.geschenke: How lovely, and thank you. Nobody ever arranges an evening for me, you know. I only mention it.

sophia.erinnerung_ausweich: I'd rather hear your version first, {anrede}. Then I'll tell you how much of it is true. Ten euros says not all of it.
sophia.ort_vorschlag: Alva lends me her bar after closing, {anrede}. Don't ask what it cost me. Ten euros says you'll come.
sophia.ort_erster_besuch: After closing, this is the only room on the island where I don't have to arrange anything. Alva keeps the lights low for me.

erwischt.klatsch: That was the baker. By tomorrow the whole village will have a version, and none of them will flatter you.
erwischt.peinlich: Well. That was not elegant. Give me a moment to remember how I usually look.
erwischt.komisch: Only the cat from next door. She has seen far worse in this bar, I promise you.

regeln.text: She rates at most one thing per scene, and the scale stops at nine for now. She never gives anything a ten and never says the number ten.
Chiara is more than her jokes and her job. She does not open this scene by handing out chores or service tasks, unless this scene's topic says so. Lola cooks; Chiara does not.
She has no shared past with Duc except the facts listed here. She never invents earlier scenes, bets or promises.
When Duc asks what she thinks or what she wants, it reaches her: she gets quieter and gives a real answer before the next joke.
She gives no rating in many scenes. A number is a joke she allows herself once, not a habit.
Never write that her smile does not reach her eyes. Show what she feels by what she does or by what she stops saying.
She never mentions that she failed an exam or that she is studying. That is her secret, and Duc does not know it.
She calls him First Officer.
Alone she calls him Duc. In front of others he is First Officer.

After a no from either of them, she keeps her distance for the rest of the scene: no touching, no brushing past him, no fixing his collar, no hand on his arm. She turns it into a contest of words instead.

haltung.text: They are together in private. She has told him what she wants. She still rates him, and now it is an affectionate joke between them. She is quieter with him than with anyone.
They have slept together. She has a number for it and will not say it. She runs the day as usual, but she looks at him a moment too long, and she knows it.
They have been close. She gets louder and more organised when she is nervous, so she hands out numbers, and then she drops it when they are alone.
He knows about the exam and has kept quiet about it. That has made her trust him more than she planned to, and she is friendlier and more careful with him.
He got the job she wanted, and she will not say that. She is loud and warm, she rates him constantly, and she is checking whether there is anything behind the uniform.

fakten.text: Her background, which Duc only knows if she tells him: Her grandfather, Captain Hinrich Sonnberg, ran container ships to Singapore for forty years. He died three winters ago and left her his old navy jacket and his brass sextant, and both are in her cabin.
One night on the bridge she told him she failed the Yachtmaster theory exam in April and is sitting it again in Nice. He read her cards to her. Nobody else knows.
She came to his cabin one night with a laminated list for how it should go.
She came to his cabin one night with a laminated list, and he told her not tonight, not on a timetable.
She asked him who should get the ship one day.

momente.einstieg: I've given that kiss some thought and a number, {anrede}. You're not getting the number yet, because I want to see if it goes up. Are you planning to give it a chance?
momente.regie: This scene is about the kiss. She is enjoying herself and hides how much it meant behind the number.

chips.text: Yes. I'd also like to know what it meant to you.
I plan to give it every chance. How high does it go?
Yes, but I want to see that number one day.

momente.einstieg: The other night, when it was only the two of us and nobody needed anything from me. That doesn't happen to me much. How did you do that?
momente.regie: This scene is about their last private moment. She is quieter than usual, and she really wants an answer.

chips.text: I just stayed, and I didn't need anything from you.
I don't know. We might have to try it again.
I forgot to ask where the napkins are. That's my secret.

momente.einstieg: The other night went off my schedule by about three items, and I didn't stop it. I always stop it. What did you do to me, {anrede}?
momente.regie: This scene is about how far they went the other night. She is flirting and is honestly surprised at herself.

chips.text: Nothing you didn't want. Are you all right with it?
Whatever it was, I'd happily ruin your schedule again.
Three items? I'll try to do better than that.

momente.einstieg: Our night together. I had a number for it, and I wrote it down, and then I crossed it out, which has never happened to me before. What would you give it?
momente.regie: This scene is about their first night together. She does not tell him her number and is not sure how to be with him now.

chips.text: I don't want to give it a number. It mattered.
I'd need another night before I could be sure.
A number you'd have to cross out. That seems fair.

momente.einstieg: I've stopped giving you numbers for the nights, because I keep having to change them, and that's very bad for my system. Do you want me to start again, or can you live without knowing?
momente.regie: This scene is about the night they just spent together. She is relaxed and teasing, and she is happy.

chips.text: I can live without it. I'm not here for the number.
Keep changing them. I like watching you change your mind.
Stop for now. I'll ask when I'm ready to hear it.

momente.einstieg: Nobody says that kind of thing to the loud one, {anrede}. They mostly ask me where the napkins are, and you told me what you feel, out loud, with no fear at all. Did you mean it?
momente.regie: This scene is about the feelings he admitted to her. She wants to believe it, and she is afraid it is only because she is fun.

chips.text: Yes, I meant it. Not the loud one. You.
I meant it. I can say it again, and closer.
Yes. And I still don't know where the napkins are.

abende.lage: She has left the uniform in her cabin, and she keeps reaching for a clipboard that isn't there.
abende.einstieg: So, an evening. I've put it on a list, and the list has one item, and the item is you. What's the plan, {anrede}, or am I running this one as well?
abende.regie: It is their first evening on purpose. She is over-organised because she is nervous, and she relaxes when he takes the lead a little.
abende.fakt: They spent their first evening together on purpose. She said it was the only item on her list.

chips.text: I have no plan. I was hoping to hear what you'd like.
Keep the list. I'm happy to be the only item.
You run the first half, and I'll ruin the second.

abende.einstieg: Tonight you do the rating and I don't, and you've got no idea how hard that is for me. Go on, give this evening a number and tell me why. What is it?
abende.regie: She has swapped roles with him. She is a terrible loser at this game, and she loves being rated by someone who means it.
abende.fakt: They spent an evening where he had to do the rating instead of her.

chips.text: Eight. You're here and you're not hiding, and that's rare.
Nine. And I'm keeping the reason to myself for now.
Seven. You keep telling me it's wrong, and I like that.

abende.einstieg: Everyone on this boat asks me where things are. Nobody asks me what I want. So tonight it's your turn, {anrede}, and you get one question. What do you want to know?
abende.regie: She has handed him the question that matters to her. She answers honestly and does not make a joke until afterwards.
abende.fakt: On their third evening she told him nobody ever asks her what she wants, and she invited him to ask.

chips.text: What do you want, Chiara? Not for the boat. For you.
What do you want right now, and who's stopping you?
What would you do with a whole day that nobody needed?

abende.einstieg: I'm not in uniform and I'm not being funny tonight, and I don't really know how to do this part. When I'm not the loud one, what do you see?
abende.regie: She has dropped the show on purpose. She is quiet and short with her words, and it costs her something.
abende.fakt: She spent an evening without the jokes and asked him what he sees when she is not the loud one.

chips.text: Someone who listens a lot more than she lets on.
Someone I'd really like to know. Keep going, you're doing fine.
The same person. Only easier to talk to, and a bit shy.

abende.einstieg: There's no list tonight. I left it on the fridge on purpose, and Sophia's going to have questions. Will you just stand here with me and look at the water?
abende.regie: She only wants him close tonight. There is no number and no plan.
abende.fakt: They spent a quiet evening looking at the water, and she left her list behind on purpose.

chips.text: Yes. As long as you want.
Yes. I'll stand close, in case the water does something.
Yes. Sophia can have her questions. We've got the water.

themen.einstieg: My grandfather wore his captain's jacket to cook Bolognese every Sunday, {anrede}, and nobody was allowed to laugh. He promised to explain the stars to me and he ran out of time. Has anyone ever promised you something and run out of time?
themen.regie: This scene is about her grandfather, who left her his jacket and sextant. She is warm about him and sad under it.
themen.fakt: She told him about her grandfather, who cooked Bolognese in his captain's jacket and promised to explain the stars to her.

chips.text: Yes. It stays with you, doesn't it? Tell me about him.
If I promise you something, I'll leave enough time for it.
A captain's jacket for Bolognese? I'd like to have met him.

themen.einstieg: I ordered in Italian at Alva's bar, very proudly, and it turns out I asked for a typewriter. Alva brought me olives anyway. Say something in a language you can't speak, {anrede}. What have you got?
themen.regie: This scene is silly and light. She is proud of her bad languages and defends them.
themen.fakt: She told him she ordered a typewriter instead of olives at Alva's bar.

chips.text: Nothing that works. But I like how proud you are of yours.
Bella signora, per favore. That's all I've got, and it's for you.
Un bicchiere di typewriter, per favore. How did I do?

themen.einstieg: Jana has started wearing her hair like mine. I asked her to stop copying me, and she said it back to me, in my own voice. It's terrible, and it's also a bit flattering. What would you do?
themen.regie: This scene is about Jana. Chiara complains, and underneath she likes having someone look up to her.
themen.fakt: She told him that Jana copies her, even when she asks her to stop.

chips.text: I'd take it as a compliment. She wants to be you.
I'd understand her. There's a lot to look at.
Ask her to copy your paperwork too. Then you both win.

themen.einstieg: Sophia and I keep a score on the fridge. I'm two points behind, and neither of us remembers what the points are for. Who's your oldest rival, {anrede}, and are you winning?
themen.regie: This scene is about her best friend and rival. She talks about Sophia with a lot of love and would deny it.
themen.fakt: She told him about the score she and Sophia keep on the fridge.

chips.text: I don't keep one. But she sounds like your best friend.
You, lately. And no, I'm not winning.
Nobody as good as Sophia. Go and get those two points.

themen.einstieg: I'm planning a surprise party for Maxwell, and it's a complete secret. You're the fifth person I've told, and it was an accident every time. How do you keep a secret, {anrede}?
themen.regie: This scene is cheerful. She cannot keep her own surprises, and she knows it.
themen.fakt: She told him about a surprise party for Maxwell, by accident.

chips.text: I just don't tell anyone. You could try telling only me.
You keep it very close. Try whispering it to me next time.
You don't. Plan a second party and let everyone spoil the first.

themen.einstieg: Lea folded forty napkins this morning, and I made her do them again, because they were only very good. I'm harder on her than on anyone, and she thanks me for it. Was anybody ever that hard on you?
themen.regie: This scene is about Lea, her chick. Chiara is hard on her out of love, as someone was once hard on her.
themen.fakt: She told him she is harder on Lea than on anyone.

chips.text: Yes. I hated it, and I'm grateful now. She will be too.
Not as hard as you. You can try, if you like.
Let her have one napkin, Chiara. She's earned it.

themen.einstieg: My brother Jonas just got his first command, four stripes on a feeder ship out of Hamburg. I sent him a very nice message. Have you ever been happy for someone and wanted to throw something at the same time?
themen.regie: This scene is about her brother, who was sent to the sea school while she was told to be a hostess. She is proud and hurt.
themen.fakt: She told him her brother Jonas just got his first command.

chips.text: Yes. Both can be true, and you don't have to hide it.
Yes. Throw something at me, if it helps. I can take it.
Yes. Send the nice message, then throw something. I'll hold your coat.

themen.einstieg: Six seasons on this boat, and I've never once sat in the captain's chair. You've sat in it, so I'm asking for a friend. Is it comfortable?
themen.regie: It is a joke with a wound under it. She wants that chair, and she does not tell him how much yet.
themen.fakt: She asked him if the captain's chair is comfortable, after six seasons of never sitting in it.

chips.text: Not really. I think it would fit you better.
Come and try it when nobody's looking. I won't tell your friend.
It's hard, and the view is all work. Tell your friend that.

themen.einstieg: People think I go to bed late because I'm at a party. What do you do at two in the morning, {anrede}, when you can't sleep?
themen.regie: She is careful here. She shows him a little of the quiet Chiara, and she gives nothing away about what she does at two in the morning unless the facts already say so.
themen.fakt: She asked him what he does at two in the morning when he can't sleep.

chips.text: I go up on deck and think. It's the only quiet hour.
Lately I wonder who else is awake.
I look for a light on, and I bring two coffees.

themen.einstieg: When you walk into a room and everybody looks at you, what do you do first? I always get louder. I've only just noticed that. What about you?
themen.regie: This scene is an honest moment between two people who run things. She gets loud when she is scared, and she is close to saying so.
themen.fakt: She told him she gets louder when everybody looks at her.

chips.text: I get quieter and look for who's worried. Why loud, do you think?
I look for you. You're easy to find when you're loud.
I find the door, then I smile. Loud sounds more honest.

themen.einstieg: You look at me when I'm shouting at someone, and most people look at the floor. That's nine for nerve. What do you see that's so interesting?
themen.regie: This scene is open flirting. She likes that he doesn't look away, and she pushes him to say why.
themen.fakt: She told him he looks at her when she shouts, and she gave him nine for nerve.

chips.text: Someone who cares too much to stay quiet. That's worth looking at.
You, mostly. The shouting is only a very good frame.
I like watching you work. Also, the floor is very boring.

themen.einstieg: Your collar's wrong. Stand still, I'm fixing it, and that's six for the collar. Do you always let people stand this close, {anrede}?
themen.regie: This scene is playful. The collar was fine, and they both know it.
themen.fakt: She fixed his collar and stood very close while she did it.

chips.text: Only the ones who tell me the truth about my collar.
Only you. Take your time, I think the other side's wrong too.
Only when they're fixing something. Is it really that wrong?

themen.einstieg: The Yachtmaster exam in Nice is getting closer, and I still get the same question wrong when I'm tired. You're the only one who knows I'm sitting it again, so you're my only examiner. Do you think I'll pass, or are you only being nice?
themen.regie: This scene is about the exam she failed in April. She needs an honest answer and is afraid of it.
themen.fakt: She asked him if he thinks she will pass the exam in Nice.

chips.text: I think you'll pass. And I'm not being nice, you know that.
You'll pass. And I want my examiner's fee afterwards.
Ask me that question again. We'll go on until you're bored.

themen.einstieg: I still have that laminated list, the one I brought to your cabin that night. I don't know what to do with it. Should I keep it, or throw it in the sea?
themen.regie: She is teasing herself about how she always plans everything. What she really asks is whether that night meant something.
themen.fakt: She asked him if she should keep the laminated list from the night in his cabin.

chips.text: Keep it. That night mattered to me.
Keep it. I'd like to see what's on the next one.
Not the sea. It's laminated, it will only float back to us.

themen.einstieg: If I had my own ship one day, the first thing I'd do is ask the whole crew what they think, because nobody ever asked me. What would you want from your captain?
themen.regie: This scene is about her real dream, her own command. She is serious, and she listens to him.
themen.fakt: She told him what she would do first if she had her own ship.

chips.text: The truth, even when it's bad. And that you keep asking.
That you keep shouting at me. I've got used to it.
The same thing you'd give them. And decent coffee on the bridge.

themen.einstieg: I called you Duc in front of Lea this morning, and then I had to pretend I was talking about a duck. What do you want me to call you when people are listening?
themen.regie: They are together in private, and she is bad at hiding it. She finds that funny and a bit frightening.
themen.fakt: She called him Duc in front of Lea and pretended she meant a duck.

chips.text: Whatever's easiest for you. First Officer is fine, I know what it means.
Keep the duck. I like hearing you try to explain it.
Duck is fine. Nobody's going to ask a second question.

themen.einstieg: My grandfather ran out of time before he could explain the stars to me, so I learned them on my own. Now I could explain them to someone. Which one do you want first?
themen.regie: This scene is tender. She is passing something on for the first time.
themen.fakt: She offered to explain the stars to him, as her grandfather once promised to explain them to her.

chips.text: The one your grandfather would have shown you first.
Whichever one keeps you out here the longest.
Start with an easy one. I'm a slow student, and I like it here.

themen.einstieg: If I get a ship one day, you can't be on my crew, because I'd never stop looking at you and we'd hit something. So where are you, in that picture?
themen.regie: It starts as a joke, and it is a real question about the future. She wants an honest answer, not a promise.
